title: Six Forgotten Heritage Sites Bollywood Brought Back Into the Spotlight
excerpt: From Kashmir's 8th-century Martand Sun Temple to Rajasthan's thousand-year-old stepwells, iconic films like Haider, Lagaan and Paheli turned overlooked heritage sites into cinematic landmarks — and in at least one case, boosted real tourism.
body:
• An Architectural Digest India roundup flags six overlooked heritage sites that iconic Bollywood films turned into on-screen landmarks — from a 1,200-year-old stepwell to an 18th-century palace in Hooghly.
  • The films span three decades of Hindi cinema: Lagaan (2001), Paheli (2005), Lootera (2013), Haider (2014), Tumbbad (2018) and Brahmāstra (2022).
  • The clearest proof of the "film tourism" effect: Vishal Bhardwaj revealed that the "Bismil" song in Haider caused a spike in footfall at Kashmir's Martand Sun Temple, prompting the ASI to clear encroachments from the site.
  • For diaspora travelers, these are ready-made itineraries: several sites — like the Martand temple and the stepwells of Abhaneri and Tonk — are within a few hours of major cities.

Bollywood has always loved palaces and forts. But the industry's most memorable location work often happens at places Indian audiences barely know — 300-year-old stepwells, decaying Maratha wadas, an 18th-century palace on the Hooghly river. An Architectural Digest India roundup highlights six such heritage sites that iconic films rescued from obscurity, and each is worth knowing for the history alone.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=qe72_BaMdeE

1. Vijaya Vilas Palace & Prag Mahal — Lagaan (2001)

Ashutosh Gowariker's Oscar-nominated epic did not rely on studio sets for its fictional Champaner village. It shot at two real palaces in Gujarat: Vijaya Vilas Palace in Mandvi, built in the 1920s by Rao Vijayrajji, and Prag Mahal in Bhuj, commissioned in 1865 by Rao Pragmalji II and designed by British architect Colonel Henry Saint Wilkins in Italian Gothic style. Both remain among Kutch's most photogenic royal residences.

2. Chand Baori & Hadi Rani ki Baori — Paheli (2005)

Shah Rukh Khan's ghost-folk tale used two of Rajasthan's most extraordinary stepwells. Chand Baori at Abhaneri, one of the largest and deepest stepwells in India, was commissioned around the 8th–9th century by King Chanda of the Nikumbha dynasty; its 3,500 steps descend 13 stories in a geometric grid. Hadi Rani ki Baori at Tonk, a 17th-century stepwell named for the Rajput queen who died for her husband's honor, gave the film its haunting interiors.

3. Itachuna Rajbari, Hooghly — Lootera (2013)

Vikramaditya Motwane's period romance found its authentic 1950s zamindar estate in Itachuna Rajbari, the 18th-century palace in West Bengal's Hooghly district. Built in 1766 by the ancestors of the Kundu family — Maratha traders who settled in Bengal after the "Bargee" raids of the 1740s — the palace spans 20 acres of courtyards and a family deity hall. Today it operates as a heritage homestay, and its owners stopped film shoots around 2015 over concerns about damage. Deulghata's 11th-century Jain temples in Purulia, also featured in the film, add an even older layer to the story.

"It is sad that we need a movie set as a reference point to what was once a spectacular Sun temple, unlike any, anywhere in the subcontinent."

— Live History India, on the Martand Sun Temple

4. Martand Sun Temple, Kashmir — Haider (2014)

The setting of Vishal Bhardwaj's haunting "Bismil" song in Haider is one of India's oldest sun temples. The Martand Sun Temple, near Anantnag in Kashmir, was built in the 8th century CE by Lalitaditya Muktapida, the Karkota-dynasty emperor of Kashmir's golden age. Dedicated to Surya, the limestone complex blended Indian, Chinese, Roman and Greek influences in a footprint some 220 feet long. It was demolished on the orders of Sultan Sikandar Shah Miri in the 15th century. The film gave the ruin a second life: Bhardwaj revealed that "Bismil" triggered a surge of visitors, enough for the Archaeological Survey of India to remove encroachments from the site.

5. Purandare Wada, Saswad — Tumbbad (2018)

The horror-fable Tumbbad needed a building that felt cursed, and found it in Purandare Wada, the decaying 18th-century Maratha-era mansion in Saswad, Maharashtra, built by the Purandare family — once close associates of the Peshwas. Its mossy arches, broken beams and shadowy corridors were the wada's own aged fabric, used as visual metaphors for greed and decay.

6. Ramnagar Fort, Varanasi — Brahmāstra (2022)

Ayan Mukerji's fantasy spectacle borrowed its mythic scale from Ramnagar Fort, the 18th-century fortified palace of the Kashi Naresh on the eastern bank of the Ganges in Varanasi. Built around 1750 by Raja Balwant Singh, the fort is still the royal family's residence, with its ornate Durbar Hall, Sanskrit museum and vintage car collection.

Why This Matters Beyond the Screen

Filmmakers and heritage professionals argue that cinema performs a real archival function. As Lucknow-based production manager Iqbal Kidwai has noted, "twenty or twenty-five years down the line, when half these places won't exist, such documentation will be precious." Producer Anand Pandit recently made the same case for today's cinema.

For the diaspora planning a heritage trip, the list doubles as an itinerary: the Kutch palaces pair with a White Rann visit, the Rajasthan stepwells are day trips from Jaipur, and the Martand temple is an easy detour from Srinagar. Cinema gave these places their close-ups. The history is what will keep you there.
nri_angle: A ready-made heritage itinerary for diaspora travelers — these are sites you can actually visit on the next India trip, each carrying both a film credit and real history.
author: Diaspora Desk
